approval_evidence_contract.author: safety_engineer
approval_evidence_contract.supersedes: The blanket prohibition in corpus.py rules human_approval_rejected, production_authorized_rejected and verification_credit_rejected, under which an approval value failed validation however it was formed. This block is the replacement. corpus.py reads it; it is not a copy of a constant held in the tool.

human_approval.grant_is: any value other than "pending" or absent; that is a recorded human decision

required_elements: 1. the approval field itself set to its grant value

2. approval_evidence.<kind>.approved_by - a named individual, not a role and not a team: at least two whitespace-separated tokens, not equal to any role_id or role name declared in this file's roles[] (case-insensitive), no token equal to a role_id, and no token from the team vocabulary (team, group, board, committee, panel, crew, squad, pool, department, office, the, staff, reviewers, approvers, automation, system, tool, script, agent, bot)

3. approval_evidence.<kind>.role - a role_id declared in this file's roles[] - together with approval_evidence.<kind>.independence, an object carrying owner_role (must equal the record's own owner_role), satisfied (true), evidence (a non-empty explanation of how independence holds, not a placeholder), and policy_ref (must name this file and the role_id)
4. approval_evidence.<kind>.date - ISO-8601, a date or a date-time

5. approval_evidence.<kind>.review_packet - an object carrying path (a packet.json under docs/artifacts/reviews/packets/ or the signed-packet archive at docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/, relative to the repository root, and present on disk), sha256 (the sha256 of that file's bytes as they are on disk now), and record_sha256_at_signing (must equal the packet's own integrity.record_sha256). The packet must also name this record in target.record_id and target.profile, and its integrity.record_path must resolve to this record's own file.

6. a revision_history entry whose author is the approving role, whose revision is at least the record's current revision, and whose description both records the approval and references the signed packet by digest or by path
approval_evidence_contract.independence_rule: The approving role must differ from the record's owner_role AND from the author of the last revision_history entry that CHANGED the record's content. An entry whose description records the approval is not a content change and is skipped when the author is determined, so an approval does not disqualify its own signer by bumping the revision. A record cannot be approved by the person or role that wrote the content being approved.

production_authority_roles.basis: Declared here rather than inferred from the free-text authority strings in roles[], because matching prose is not measurement. architect is declared 'full authority over corpus artifacts' and carries 'final evaluation'; safety_manager is declared to 'approve safety case'. No other role in roles[] is given authority to release the corpus to production.

production_authorizable_artifact_types.basis: review_policy.additional_fields.human_approval_required_for names safety_case, production_release and change_approval as the three things human approval is required for. post_development_record is this corpus's artifact_type for a production_release record. Production authority is therefore expressible only on those three families; on any other family the grant fails even with complete evidence, because the record is not one human approval is required for.

unchanged_by_this_amendment: human_approval_status 'not_required' is still rejected. It is not an approval value, so this contract does not speak to it, and the pre-existing governance_authority_claim test that treats every non-pending value as a claim continues to fire on it. Relaxing it is a separate decision the corpus owner has not taken.

The recursive authority_keys scan (production_release, authorized_for_production and eight siblings) and the four GOVERNANCE_CLAIM_FIELDS claim classes (ASIL determination, conformity, certification) are untouched. This amendment changes only what a properly evidenced approval is ALLOWED to say; it adds no new authority.
No record in this corpus carries an approval. The contract describes how one would be recorded. It does not record one.

approval_ledger_contract.author: safety_engineer
approval_ledger_contract.supersedes: Element 6 of approval_evidence_contract.required_elements as written by APPROVAL-RULE-A1, which required 'a revision_history entry whose author is the approving role, whose revision is at least the record's current revision, and whose description both records the approval and references the signed packet by digest or by path'. That requirement is withdrawn, not deleted: its text is preserved above, in approval_evidence_contract.required_elements[5], and the reason it had to be withdrawn is recorded under previous_meaning and under element_6_withdrawal_reason below. Nothing else is superseded. Elements 1-5, the independence_rule, the production-authority bar and the whole of APPROVAL-RULE-A1 stand unaltered.
approval_ledger_contract.effective_note: corpus.py reads THIS block in preference to approval_evidence_contract when this flag is true, so the six required elements the tool enforces are the six below and not the six above. A superseded element list is kept in the file rather than edited in place, because an amendment that is rewritten cannot be audited.
approval_ledger_contract.element_6_withdrawal_reason: Recording the approval in revision_history forces a revision bump, and a revision bump breaks two controls that nothing authorised breaking: every link that pins that record's revision goes stale, and every review record stores a sha256 of that record, so the sha256 is invalidated. Measured, not assumed - see closing-list.md 1.6 P3 and coverage-plan.json CORR-COV-023. The consequence of the amendment that introduced the six elements was therefore that a legitimately evidenced approval could not be recorded at all without collateral damage, and the tool's own happy-path self-test had to pick a record that no review digest covers in order to prove the approval validates at all. That is the signature of an unsatisfiable requirement, not of a working one.
required_elements: 1. the approval field itself set to its grant value

2. approval_evidence.<kind>.approved_by - a named individual, not a role and not a team: at least two whitespace-separated tokens, not equal to any role_id or role name declared in this file's roles[] (case-insensitive), no token equal to a role_id, and no token from the team vocabulary (team, group, board, committee, panel, crew, squad, pool, department, office, the, staff, reviewers, approvers, automation, system, tool, script, agent, bot)

3. approval_evidence.<kind>.role - a role_id declared in this file's roles[] - together with approval_evidence.<kind>.independence, an object carrying owner_role (must equal the record's own owner_role), satisfied (true), evidence (a non-empty explanation of how independence holds, not a placeholder), and policy_ref (must name this file and the role_id)
4. approval_evidence.<kind>.date - ISO-8601, a date or a date-time

5. approval_evidence.<kind>.review_packet - an object carrying path (a packet.json under the SIGNED-PACKET ARCHIVE at docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/ ONLY, relative to the repository root, and present on disk; a citation into docs/artifacts/reviews/packets/ is REJECTED because that tree is regenerated and would destroy the evidence), sha256 (the sha256 of that file's bytes as they are on disk now), and record_sha256_at_signing (must equal the packet's own integrity.record_sha256). The packet must also name this record in target.record_id and target.profile, and its integrity.record_path must resolve to this record's own file.

6. approval_ledger_ref - an object on the record naming the append-only ledger entry that records this approval: ledger_id (the entry's own id in docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl) and entry_sha256 (the digest of that entry). The entry must exist, must name this record's (profile, id), must carry this approval's kind, and its approved_record_sha256 must equal this record's CURRENT CONTENT digest. approval_ledger_ref is APPROVAL METADATA, not content: it is excluded from the content digest, it is never a revision_history entry, and recording it does not bump the record's revision. An approval is therefore recorded in the ledger and nowhere else, and recording one neither stales a link nor invalidates a review digest.

ledger.format: JSON Lines, append-only, one JSON object per line, in approval order. Lines are never reordered and never removed. The file as committed is EMPTY: this corpus holds no approval.
ledger.append_only_note: The ledger is append-only by construction: an entry names its predecessor by digest, so removing, reordering or editing any entry breaks the chain from that point on and the validator reports the first break. There is no code path in this repository that appends to the ledger, and none may be added without a person.
required_entry_fields: kind - one of the kinds in approval_evidence_contract.kinds
approved_record_sha256 - the CONTENT digest of the record at the moment of signing (see content_digest_rule)
approved_content_revision - the record's content revision at the moment of signing
approved_by - a named individual, under the same element-2 rule as on the record
role - a role_id declared in this file's roles[]
independence - the same object the record carries, under the same element-3 rule
signed_packet - an object carrying path (under docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/) and sha256 (that file's bytes as committed)
packet_first_commit - the 40-hex git commit that FIRST contained signed_packet.path; the validator confirms the commit exists and that the blob is present in it
previous_entry_sha256 - the digest of the preceding entry, or 64 zeros for the first entry
ledger.content_digest_rule: The content digest of a record is the sha256 of its bytes with approval metadata removed. A record that carries no approval_ledger_ref therefore has content digest == sha256 of its file bytes, which is what every one of the 321 records in this corpus reads today, so nothing already verified changes. A record that does carry approval_ledger_ref has the field stripped and is re-serialised canonically. This is the mechanism by which recording an approval leaves every stored review digest valid: the approval is metadata about a record, not a change to it.
ledger.chain_rule: entries[i].previous_entry_sha256 == sha256(canonical_json(entries[i-1])) for every i > 0, and entries[0].previous_entry_sha256 == 64 zeros. canonical_json is UTF-8 JSON with sorted keys and no insignificant whitespace. The chain proves EXISTENCE, ORDER and INTEGRITY of the entries. It does not prove a human read anything.
ledger.staleness_rule: An entry whose approved_record_sha256 no longer equals the record's current content digest is STALE. STALE IS NOT INVALID: it must not fail validation. It must be reported, counted in the approval_staleness coverage metric as stale/total, and named in a finding that says which record, which ledger entry, and which fields changed - recoverable because every signed packet embeds the approved record verbatim under record_verbatim, so the validator diffs the approved bytes against the current ones rather than reporting two opaque digests.
ledger.stale_approval_and_the_numerator: A stale approval is not counted in the human_approval numerator, because the numerator means 'records carrying an approval that describes the bytes now on disk' and a stale one does not. It is not discarded either: approval_staleness accounts for it, and the two figures together account for every approval in the ledger. Nothing is silently dropped.
ledger.anchored_to_version_history_meaning: packet_first_commit proves WHEN the signed packet was first committed and IN WHAT STATE - that the bytes the reviewer signed existed in this repository at a known point in its history. It proves nothing about who read them.

approval_ledger_contract.residual_limit_that_this_does_not_reduce: THE CHAIN PROVES EXISTENCE, ORDERING AND INTEGRITY. IT DOES NOT PROVE A HUMAN READ ANYTHING, AND IT DOES NOT MAKE AN APPROVAL UNFORGEABLE. A determined person can still write all six elements, archive a packet, cite a real commit and maintain the chain correctly; nothing in this repository can distinguish that from an approval a competent independent reviewer genuinely gave. That limit is IRREDUCIBLE, not mitigated: any attestation can be forged by someone determined to lie, and the cost of forging it has been raised rather than removed. Do not describe the hash chain, the git anchor or the archive rule as making approval unforgeable.
unchanged_by_this_amendment: No record in this corpus carries an approval, and the ledger is empty. This block describes how one WOULD be recorded. It does not record one.
Elements 1-5, the independence_rule, the production-authority bar and APPROVAL-RULE-A1 in its entirety are unchanged.
human_approval_status 'not_required' is still rejected, for want of evidence. That remains open P3 in closing-list.md 1.6.
The recursive authority_keys scan and the four GOVERNANCE_CLAIM_FIELDS claim classes are untouched.

approval_countersignature_contract.author: safety_engineer
approval_countersignature_contract.previous_text: An approval carried ONE signature. docs/artifacts/governance/role-and-review-policy.json#/approval_evidence_contract/required_elements[1..5] named one approver, one role, one independence assertion, one date and one signed packet; approval_ledger_contract/ledger/required_entry_fields named approved_by, role, independence, date and signed_packet. Nothing in either contract required a second party, so one person could satisfy the whole contract alone.
approval_countersignature_contract.why_this_is_needed: The six-element contract, the hash chain and the git anchor all detect TAMPERING WITH THE RECORD. None of them prevents one determined person writing a self-consistent ledger entry, a real packet and a real commit - which is exactly what the independent checker's own output says. Every one of those layers binds ONE signature; a single binding is satisfied by a single forger. Adding a second, independent signature does not make the approval unforgeable, because nothing can. It changes the shape of the forgery from 'one person acting alone' to 'two people who are independent of each other and of the content, both choosing to lie', and it is a materially harder thing to do quietly.
approval_countersignature_contract.rule: AN APPROVAL REQUIRES TWO SIGNATURES. The record's approval_evidence.<kind> carries a `countersignature` object beside the approver's own evidence, and the ledger entry carries the same `countersignature`. Both go in the SAME ledger entry, so the hash chain binds them together: editing or removing either one breaks the chain at that entry and every entry after it. The countersignature carries the full six-element evidence in its own right - the grant being countersigned (the entry's own kind and record_id), a named individual as `approved_by`, a declared `role_id`, an `independence` object judged against THIS record's owner_role, an ISO-8601 `date`, and a `review_packet` whose `record_sha256_at_signing` is the SAME digest the approver attested. Not the same PATH necessarily, but the same DIGEST: two people signed the same bytes of the same revision, which is the only thing that makes a countersignature a countersignature rather than a second, unrelated review.
approval_countersignature_contract.countersigner_independence_rule: The countersigner's role must satisfy ALL FIVE clauses, each checked separately so a rejection names which one failed. (1) It is a role_id declared in this file's roles[]. (2) It is not the record's own owner_role. (3) It is not the author of ANY revision_history entry that changed this record's content at or below the revision being approved - every such author, not only the most recent one, because a countersigner is held to a stronger authorship test than an approver is: an approver is excluded from the last content revision only, a countersigner from all of them. (4) It is not the approver's own role, so the two signatures cannot be two roles wearing one name. (5) It is not listed in countersigner_excluded_roles_by_owner_role[<the record's owner_role>], which is the per-owner_role part of the requirement. Alongside these: (6) the countersigner's name must not be the approver's name, compared on normalised token sets so that 'Ada Lovelace' and 'A. Lovelace' are treated as one person and rejected; (7) the countersigner must not be a role name or a team name, on the same grounds as the approver.
approval_countersignature_contract.countersigner_excluded_roles_basis: Declared per owner_role rather than computed, so the requirement is a policy statement the enforcing code reads rather than an inference it makes. The pattern is that where an owner role sits inside one half of a PAIR that checks the other's work, its counterpart in that pair may not countersign it: sw_engineer is excluded from hw_engineer's records and vice versa, because the two write the two halves of the same partition and each is the other's first reviewer; the same holds for sw_engineer against system_engineer and system_engineer against hw_engineer. For safety_engineer, verification_engineer, traceability_engineer, architect, project_manager and the two reviewer roles no exclusion is declared, because those roles do not pair with an owner role in the same way - a safety record's countersigner may be a verification engineer, a traceability engineer or an architect, and any of those is genuinely external to it.
approval_countersignature_contract.unmapped_owner_role_policy: Where the record's owner_role is a key this file does not declare - there are eight on disk at the time of writing (change_manager, configuration_manager, cybersecurity_engineer, data_quality_engineer, integration_engineer, quality_engineer, sys_engineer, verification_lead), none of them declared in roles[] - clauses (1) to (4) and (6) and (7) still apply in full, and the per-owner_role clause (5) has an empty exclusion set. That is recorded rather than hidden: inventing a role definition for an undeclared owner_role is a vocabulary decision nobody has taken, and this corpus has already declined to invent one (see the controlled vocabulary record's migration reasoning). Adding these eight roles to roles[] and to the map above is the follow-up, and until it happens a countersignature on a quality_engineer-owned record is checked strictly less than on a sw_engineer-owned one. That gap is stated here rather than closed by guessing.
required_fields: approved_by - a named individual, on the same rules as the approver's: at least two tokens, not a role_id, not a role name, not a team name from the machine vocabulary
role - a role_id declared in roles[], subject to all five independence clauses above

independence - an object carrying owner_role equal to this record's own owner_role, satisfied true, a non-placeholder evidence string of at least the same minimum length as the approver's, and a policy_ref citing this file
date - an ISO-8601 date or date-time, grammar- and parse-checked

review_packet - path plus sha256 plus record_sha256_at_signing, where record_sha256_at_signing EQUALS the approver's, the path resolves to a packet.json on disk under docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/ whose own integrity.record_sha256 equals that digest, and whose target.record_id and target.profile name this record
approval_countersignature_contract.where_it_is_checked: Two places, both reading this block rather than restating it. (1) corpus.py _approval_evidence_defects, as element 7, so element 7 is reached by _validate_artifact AND by _validate_governance_semantics - the path acceptance gate [7/8] runs and which never calls _validate_artifact - and therefore cannot be blind to it. (2) corpus.py _validate_approval_ledger, per entry, so a ledger entry that omits or malforms its countersignature is reported against the ledger itself rather than only against a record that references it.
what_this_does_not_do: IT DOES NOT MAKE AN APPROVAL UNFORGEABLE. Two signatures raise the cost of forgery and change its required shape. They do not prevent it, and no text anywhere in this repository describes them as preventing it.

IT DOES NOT RECORD AN APPROVAL. The ledger holds zero entries and every record keeps human_approval_status pending, production_authorized false and product_verification_credit false. This block describes how one WOULD be recorded; it records none.

IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH THAT TWO NAMES ARE TWO PEOPLE. The countersigner must not carry the approver's name, compared on normalised token sets. A person who writes a second false name on the same entry satisfies that check exactly as a second person would. This is part of the irreducible residual, and it is the reason the contract says two independent signatures rather than two signatures.

IT DOES NOT WEAKEN ANY EXISTING CONTROL. Elements 1-6, the independence rule, the production-authority bar, the chain, the anchor and the archive rule are unchanged. Element 7 is additional: it can only turn a previously-accepting single-signature approval into a rejection, never the reverse.
IT DOES NOT NARROW THE COUNT OF APPROVALS. human_approval, production_authorization and approval_staleness all read 0 and continue to read 0, for the same reason they did before: nothing is approved.
approval_countersignature_contract.residual_limit_that_this_does_not_reduce: THE RESIDUAL MOVES; IT DOES NOT CLOSE. ONE FORGER IS NO LONGER ENOUGH. Under the single-signature contract a determined person acting alone could satisfy every clause, because every clause bound one signature and one signature was all that was asked for. Under this contract a forgery requires TWO people to both be named, both hold roles independent of the record's owner_role and of every content author, both attest the same packet digest, and both appear in one ledger entry whose chain stays intact. That is a real increase in cost and a real change in the kind of act required. IT IS NOT PREVENTION. TWO COLLUDING PARTIES ARE STILL ENOUGH, and they may collude trivially: one writes both names, in two role-shaped forms of a fiction, and every machine check in this repository passes. AND NO NUMBER OF SIGNATURES FIXES IT: a third signature would require three colluding parties, a fourth four, and the limit does not move toward zero, because the binding is not how many people signed but whether any of them read anything. THE LIMIT IS THAT ATTESTATION IS NOT PROOF OF COMPREHENSION. A signature says a person asserts; it does not say a person understood, and nothing in a hash chain, a git anchor, a role declaration or a second name converts an assertion into an understanding. The honest statement of what two signatures buy is therefore: one forger is no longer sufficient, two colluding parties are, and the residual is irreducible at every arity.
unchanged_by_this_amendment: APPROVAL-RULE-A1 is left byte-for-byte intact, and APPROVAL-LEDGER-A1's replacement of element 6 is untouched. This block ADDS element 7 and adds one required ledger field; it withdraws nothing.
No record in this corpus carries an approval, an approval_evidence block, a countersignature or an approval_ledger_ref, and the ledger is empty.
The hash chain binds both signatures together because both live in the same entry. It is not two chains and not two entries.

human_approval_not_required_decision.author: safety_engineer
human_approval_not_required_decision.decides: Open item P3 in docs/artifacts/governance/closing-list.md 1.6: whether human_approval_status 'not_required' should remain rejected.
human_approval_not_required_decision.decision: LEGITIMATE. It is permitted, and it is permitted ONLY on a record whose artefact type genuinely does not require human approval. It is NOT a grant and NEVER counts toward the human_approval numerator.
human_approval_not_required_decision.previous_text: human_approval_status: 'not_required' is deliberately NOT relaxed. It is not an approval value, so the contract does not speak to it, and it still fails for want of evidence - which preserves the current verdict for that value rather than quietly changing it as a side effect of the ledger amendment. It was treated as a grant by the same test that treats 'approved' and 'rejected' as grants (any value other than 'pending'), so it was rejected by human_approval_rejected at elements 1-6.
human_approval_not_required_decision.previous_meaning: The corpus had exactly one reachable value for human_approval_status that was both schema-valid and not a validation error: 'pending'. 'not_required' was in the schema enum and in this file's own approval_semantics.human_approval_status_values, and the validator rejected it - an inconsistency rather than a policy choice. It was rejected for a coherent reason and the wrong one: the rejection was correct (a record declaring no approval gate must not smuggle an approval past the evidence contract) but arrived by treating the value as a claim of approval and then failing it for want of one. Nobody had decided whether the value was legitimate at all, so it sat open, and CORR-COV-022 and CORR-COV-023 each recorded it as still open.
reasoning: THE POLICY ITSELF ALREADY SCOPES IT. review_policy.additional_fields.human_approval_required_for is a POSITIVE LIST: safety_case, production_release, change_approval. Human approval is required for those three and, on the plain reading of a positive list, for nothing else. The corpus could enforce that list negatively - a bare 'approved' fails - but had no way to record its complement, so the scoping the policy declares had NO representation in the data model. That is the defect, and it is a defect in the corpus rather than in the value.

IT MADE TWO DIFFERENT STATES INDISTINGUISHABLE. A record on a family with no approval gate and a record waiting for an approval that will never come BOTH read 'pending'. A reviewer looking at a test measure could not tell whether it was waiting for a sign-off nobody would ever give or genuinely had no gate. That ambiguity pushes people towards workarounds, and a workaround for a governance model is more expensive than the governance model.

IT WAS NEVER RELAXED 'JUST IN CASE'. It is permitted on the complement of the very list that says where approval is required, judged against approval_evidence_contract/production_authorizable_artifact_types - the same list, and the same policy-file mapping, that already governs production authority. Inventing a second list here would be the drift CORR-COV-021 identified: a mapping enforced by code and stated in prose with nothing keeping them equal. So the relaxation is confined to the families the policy says are outside the gate.

THE EVASION IS CLOSED ON EXACTLY THE RECORDS WHERE IT MATTERS. The obvious abuse is relabelling a pending record 'not_required' to dodge a future approval requirement. That abuse is available only on a family that requires approval, and there it is REJECTED, at high severity, by the rule id human_approval_not_required_misdeclared. On a family with no gate there is nothing to dodge: no approval was ever owed. Two further contradictions are rejected for the same reason - a 'not_required' record carrying an approval_evidence.human_approval block, and one carrying an approval_ledger_ref resolving to a human_approval ledger entry. Both assert an approval exists while the record asserts none is required, and the corpus cannot tell which of the two statements is wrong, so it reports rather than picks.

IT CANNOT MOVE THE NUMERATOR. 'not_required' is excluded from _is_approval_grant, so it is never 'granted', never 'evidenced', never 'evidenced_now', and the human_approval numerator cannot read higher because of it. It is also not counted as 'considered', because 'considered' means a candidate for the grant and this is explicitly not one. The DENOMINATOR IS UNCHANGED at every record carrying an id, so a record cannot be removed from the measurement by being relabelled, and the count of 'not_required' records is reported beside the dimension - machine-readably as human_approval.not_required_records - so relabelling moves a number that is on the record rather than one that is quietly not there.

IT IS NOT A REVIEW EXEMPTION, and that is the hazard worth naming. 'not_required' is easy to misread as 'no review needed'. It is not: it records that the family has no SIGN-OFF GATE. Every record in this corpus remains reviewable and 172 of 321 are currently covered by review records, including many whose family has no gate. The review mechanism is separate and unchanged - reviewed_by links and review records - and a 'not_required' record is counted by automated_review_coverage exactly like any other. A record declaring no gate and receiving no review is therefore a visible gap in the review dimension, not an excused one.

MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. On the tree this corpus ships, 0 of 321 records carry 'not_required' and 0 carry it on a required family, so both counts are measured zeros. The decision is about representability and it creates no record.
human_approval_not_required_decision.what_is_permitted: human_approval_status may be 'not_required' on any record whose artifact_type is NOT one of approval_evidence_contract/production_authorizable_artifact_types/types. That set is {safety_case, post_development_record, change} on this corpus, being the corpus's own types for the policy's {safety_case, production_release, change_approval}. All three are therefore REQUIRED to carry either 'pending' or a properly evidenced approval, never 'not_required'.
human_approval_not_required_decision.what_is_rejected: human_approval_status 'not_required' on a record whose artifact_type IS in that set (rule human_approval_not_required_misdeclared, high severity, reached by BOTH _validate_artifact and _validate_governance_semantics so acceptance gate [7/8] cannot be blind to it); and a 'not_required' record that simultaneously carries approval_evidence.human_approval or an approval_ledger_ref resolving to a human_approval entry.
what_it_does_not_do: IT DOES NOT COUNT TOWARD THE human_approval NUMERATOR, and the dimension says so in its own detail text as well as in machine-readable fields.
IT DOES NOT CHANGE THE DENOMINATOR. human_approval stays N/N over every record carrying an id.

IT DOES NOT RELAX ANYTHING ELSE. Elements 1-6, element 7 (APPROVAL-COUNT-A1), the independence rule, the production-authority bar, the chain, the anchor and the archive rule are unchanged. 'not_required' is a new reachable state on a family that had none; it does not turn a rejection into an acceptance anywhere.
IT IS NOT A REVIEW EXEMPTION and it is not a way to close automated_review_coverage. Such a record is counted by the review-coverage dimension like any other.

IT DOES NOT RECORD ANYTHING. Every one of the 321 records keeps human_approval_status 'pending', production_authorized false and product_verification_credit false. This block describes how one WOULD be set; none is set.
human_approval_not_required_decision.detection_consequence: One new rule id, human_approval_not_required_misdeclared, added to GOVERNANCE_SEMANTIC_RULE_IDS. That moves the printed governance rule count in acceptance gate [7/8] from 8 to 9, which is a new detection capability and not a change in what any existing rule catches; the delta is reported rather than absorbed. Four self-tests: 'not_required' is accepted on a family with no gate and rejected on one with; a misdeclaration is caught through the governance path that gate [7/8] runs and that never calls _validate_artifact; it can never reach the numerator; and no record on the real tree carries it. Two coverage fields are added to the human_approval dimension: not_required_records and not_required_misdeclared.
human_approval_not_required_decision.residual_risk_recorded_here_not_silently: THE MAPPING IS THE POLICY'S, NOT THE TOOL'S. This amendment trusts approval_evidence_contract/production_authorizable_artifact_types to be the right reading of review_policy.additional_fields.human_approval_required_for. That mapping was written for production authority, where 'this family requires approval' is the condition; here it is used for its complement, which is the same boundary and therefore the same risk. If the policy's positive list is ever widened, a record type newly inside the gate must also be added to production_authorizable_artifact_types, and nothing currently ties the two lists together - a self-test asserts they are read from the same file, not that they cannot drift in meaning. SECOND: 'not_required' is one keystroke away from 'pending' and the failure mode of confusing them is quiet - a record that needed a sign-off and says it did not would be caught by the new rule, but a record that needed a sign-off and says 'pending' forever is indistinguishable from one that is simply not due yet, and no rule in this corpus detects that. THIRD: the count is 0 today, so none of this is exercised by the live tree. The self-tests are the only evidence that it works, and they are tests of the rule rather than of any approval.
